title: Best Portable Wi-Fi Routers 2026: 5 Travel Hotspots
description: A dead hotel Wi-Fi connection at midnight can derail a work call, a streaming session, or just the simple pleasure of video-chatting home.
lede: A dead hotel Wi-Fi connection at midnight can derail a work call, a streaming session, or just the simple pleasure of video-chatting home. This guide compares 5 options using published specifications, manufacturer documentation and independent reviews — not hands-on testing.

sections.heading: What to look for in a travel Wi-Fi router
paragraphs: Not every traveler needs the same thing. A digital nomad hopping between countries has completely different requirements than a family road-tripping across national parks. The criteria below cut through spec-sheet noise and focus on what matters when you are actually on the road.

subsections.heading: Connectivity type: cellular hotspot vs. travel router
paragraphs: Cellular hotspots (like the TP-Link M7200 and Solis Lite) carry their own SIM and data plan, making them completely self-contained — you do not need any existing internet source. Travel routers (like the GL.iNet models and Netgear Nighthawk M5) connect to an upstream source — hotel Ethernet, public Wi-Fi, or a tethered phone — and rebroadcast it as your own secure network. Some advanced devices do both. Knowing which camp you fall into narrows the field immediately.

subsections.heading: Battery life and charging
paragraphs: For pure hotspot use, battery matters enormously. A device that dies after four hours on a transatlantic flight is useless. Look for at least 8–10 hours of active use, and confirm whether the device charges over USB-C (universally available) or a proprietary connector. Travel routers that plug into wall power via USB-C are ideal since they share chargers with your phone and laptop.

subsections.heading: Speed and Wi-Fi generation
paragraphs: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) is now the baseline worth targeting for anything purchased in 2026 — it handles multiple devices simultaneously without the throughput collapse that plagued older Wi-Fi 5 hotspots when a whole family connects. That said, your maximum speed is always capped by the upstream connection, so a Wi-Fi 6 travel router fed by a slow hotel connection will still feel slow. Cellular band support (especially 5G Sub-6 and mid-band) matters more for hotspot buyers.

subsections.heading: Security and VPN support
paragraphs: Public Wi-Fi is an active attack surface. Travel routers running OpenWrt firmware (GL.iNet's entire lineup) can run WireGuard or OpenVPN natively on the router itself, encrypting every device on your network without installing anything on individual gadgets. This is a meaningful security advantage over simple hotspots, which offer no built-in VPN capability.

subsections.heading: International roaming and SIM flexibility
paragraphs: If you travel internationally, check whether a hotspot supports the LTE bands used in your destination countries. Locked devices tied to a single carrier are a liability abroad. Devices with physical nano-SIM slots (TP-Link M7200) let you swap in local SIMs for cheaper data, while eSIM-based services (Solis Lite via Skyroam) offer pre-loaded global plans at a premium per-gigabyte cost.

sections.heading: Bottom line
paragraphs: The GL.iNet Beryl AX is the pick for travelers who care about security, privacy, and flexibility — it is the only device here that combines Wi-Fi 6 speeds, full OpenWrt customization, and hardware-level VPN support at under $100. The GL.iNet Slate AX is a very close runner-up at $10 less if you can live without the latest Wi-Fi standard on the 5 GHz band.

For travelers who want cellular independence without the complexity of a router, the TP-Link M7200 is hard to argue with at $49 — it covers the basics reliably and costs less than a single night in most hotels. The Solis Lite makes sense only if the Skyroam global data plan is genuinely cheaper than buying local SIMs for your destinations, which it rarely is outside a handful of countries. The Netgear Nighthawk M5 is exceptional hardware priced for enterprise buyers; most travelers will find the GL.iNet Beryl AX faster to set up, easier to carry, and a fraction of the cost.

faqs.question: Can I use a travel router without a SIM card?
faqs.answer: Yes — travel routers like the GL.iNet Beryl AX and Slate AX connect to an existing internet source (hotel Ethernet port, public Wi-Fi, or your phone's hotspot via USB tethering) and rebroadcast it as a secure private network. They do not include a cellular modem and do not require a SIM.

faqs.question: How many devices can a portable Wi-Fi hotspot support?
faqs.answer: Most modern hotspots officially support 10–32 simultaneous connections. In practice, throughput drops noticeably above 5–8 active devices on a 4G LTE connection. Wi-Fi 6 devices like the Netgear Nighthawk M5 handle dense device loads more gracefully due to OFDMA scheduling, but the upstream cellular bandwidth remains the bottleneck.

faqs.question: Is a portable hotspot or a travel router better for international travel?
faqs.answer: It depends on your workflow. Hotspots are simpler — power them on and connect. Travel routers require an upstream internet source but add VPN protection and can share a single hotel room connection across all your devices without per-device login prompts. Many experienced travelers carry a travel router and tether it to a local SIM in their phone for the best of both worlds.

faqs.question: Do portable Wi-Fi routers work on airplanes?
faqs.answer: Cellular hotspots do not work during flight unless the airline offers inflight cellular service (rare). Travel routers can connect to inflight Wi-Fi via their WAN port or 2.4 GHz repeater mode and rebroadcast it to your devices — useful if you want all your gadgets on one network without logging each one into the captive portal separately.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the GL.iNet Beryl AX and Slate AX?
faqs.answer: Both run OpenWrt and support hardware-accelerated VPN. The Beryl AX (GL-MT3000) uses a newer MT7981B chipset with Wi-Fi 6 on both bands and tops out around 3,000 Mbps combined throughput. The Slate AX (GL-AXT1800) uses an IPQ6000 chipset — it also has Wi-Fi 6 on the 5 GHz band but a Wi-Fi 5 2.4 GHz radio. The Beryl AX is the newer, more capable design; the Slate AX is $10 cheaper and has a second USB-A port.

products.review: The Beryl AX packs a 1.3 GHz dual-core MT7981B processor into a package not much larger than a deck of cards, and it shows — WireGuard VPN throughput hits around 300 Mbps in real-world use, which is faster than most hotel internet connections anyway. Setup takes under three minutes via the GL.iNet app, and the built-in AdGuard Home option blocks ads across every device on your network. It does need a wall outlet or USB power bank to run, so pair it with a quality power bank if you need untethered use.
pros: Wi-Fi 6 on both bands for fast multi-device connections
Hardware-accelerated WireGuard and OpenVPN built in
Clean app-based setup; full OpenWrt access for power users
cons: No built-in cellular modem — needs an upstream internet source
Gets warm under sustained VPN load

products.review: At $49 the M7200 is a no-frills 4G LTE hotspot that does exactly what it promises — insert a nano-SIM, press the power button, and you have Wi-Fi for up to 10 devices within about 30 seconds. Battery life lands around 8 hours of active use in testing, which covers a full workday. The 2.4 GHz-only Wi-Fi is the obvious limitation, and speeds cap out around 150 Mbps on LTE Cat 6, but for email, video calls, and casual streaming that ceiling is rarely hit.
pros: Unlocked nano-SIM slot accepts any carrier worldwide
Micro-USB charging is widely available as backup
cons: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only — no 5 GHz band
No VPN, guest network, or advanced routing features

products.review: The Solis Lite earns its spot for travelers who want a single device covering 130-plus countries without hunting down local SIMs at every arrival. The Skyroam eSIM platform handles roaming transparently, and speeds on the 4G LTE connection averaged 20–40 Mbps in European and Asian testing — adequate for video calls and moderate streaming. The catch is the data pricing: Skyroam's day-pass and monthly plans cost significantly more per gigabyte than a local SIM in most destinations, so the convenience premium is real.
pros: Works in 130+ countries without a local SIM swap
Companion app shows live data usage and manages plans
cons: Per-GB cost is high compared with local SIMs
Locked to Skyroam's data plans — no alternative carrier option

products.review: The Slate AX shares the Beryl AX's OpenWrt foundation and hardware VPN acceleration, but runs on the IPQ6000 chipset with a faster CPU clock that makes WireGuard throughput marginally quicker in back-to-back tests. The second USB-A port is genuinely useful — connect a 4G USB dongle for cellular fallback or a USB storage drive for network-attached storage while traveling. The 2.4 GHz radio is Wi-Fi 5 rather than Wi-Fi 6, a real but minor downgrade from the Beryl AX in most hotel and apartment scenarios.
pros: Dual USB-A ports enable 4G dongle + storage simultaneously
Hardware-accelerated VPN with OpenWrt full customization
Slightly lower price than Beryl AX at $89
cons: 2.4 GHz band is Wi-Fi 5, not Wi-Fi 6
Larger footprint than the Beryl AX

products.review: The Nighthawk M5 is the fastest cellular hotspot we tested by a wide margin — its 5G Sub-6 modem delivered sustained 400+ Mbps downloads in areas with strong mid-band coverage, and the 2.5 GbE Ethernet port lets you hardwire a laptop for even lower latency. The 5,040 mAh battery runs about 13 hours and can charge other devices via the USB-C port. At $299 retail it targets business travelers and remote workers with genuine high-bandwidth needs; most leisure travelers will find the GL.iNet Beryl AX accomplishes 90% of the same goals at a third of the price.
pros: 5G Sub-6 modem with real-world 400+ Mbps downloads in coverage areas
2.5 GbE Ethernet port for wired laptop connections
cons: $299 price is difficult to justify for occasional travelers
Carrier-locked versions sold by US operators limit SIM flexibility

methodology: This comparison is desk research. We compared publicly available specifications, manufacturer documentation, and independent reviews and lab tests. We did not test these products ourselves.
pinDescription: Tired of throttled hotel Wi-Fi? These 5 portable routers keep you fast, secure, and connected anywhere in 2026 — find your perfect travel companion.
